passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel cognitive training program on working memory performance in adults aged 18–35. Sixty participants were randomly assigned to either the training group (n = 30) or a wait‑list control group (n = 30). Both groups completed a standardized working‑memory task (n‑back) before and after a 4‑week intervention period. The training group received daily 20‑minute sessions of adaptive n‑back exercises, while the control group received no intervention. The researchers recorded mean response times (ms) and accuracy percentages for each group at both time points. The study aimed to determine whether the training program produced measurable improvements in speed and accuracy relative to the control condition.
table_data:
Condition | Pre‑test Mean RT (ms) | Post‑test Mean RT (ms) | Pre‑test Accuracy (%) | Post‑test Accuracy (%)
Training  | 650 | 590 | 78 | 85
Control   | 652 | 648 | 77 | 78
stem: Based on the data presented, which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the effect of the training program?

options.A: The training group showed a larger pre-to-post improvement than the control group in both response time and accuracy.
options.B: Both groups exhibited similar improvements in response time, but only the training group improved in accuracy.
options.C: The control group outperformed the training group on post-test accuracy.
options.D: The training group's response time improved, but its accuracy remained unchanged.

explanation: Correct: The training group's mean RT fell 60 ms (650 to 590) and accuracy rose 7 points (78 to 85); the control group changed by only 4 ms (652 to 648) and 1 point (77 to 78). Why the others are wrong: B) The RT changes were not similar (60 ms versus 4 ms), and the control group also rose slightly in accuracy. C) Post-test accuracy was 85% for training versus 78% for control. D) Training accuracy rose from 78% to 85%.
trap: Treating the 1-point control accuracy rise as an improvement comparable to the training group's 7-point rise, or assuming significance when no test is reported.

stem: If the researchers wanted to assess whether the training program had a causal effect on working memory, which experimental design element is most critical?

options.A: Using a larger sample size of 200 participants.
options.B: Ensuring the training sessions are delivered in a double‑blind manner.
options.C: Randomly assigning participants to training and control groups.
options.D: Measuring both response time and accuracy as outcome variables.

explanation: Random assignment controls for confounding variables and allows causal inference about the training program’s effect. While a larger sample size, blinding, and multiple outcome measures are valuable, randomization is the most critical design element for establishing causality.
trap: Choosing double-blinding or a larger sample as most critical; neither establishes causation as directly as random assignment, and the passage does not describe blinding.

stem: Calculate the percent change in mean response time for the training group from pre‑ to post‑test.
explanation: Correct: A) (650 - 590)/650 x 100 = 9.2%. Why the others are wrong: B) 8.8% does not follow from the data. C) 7.5% does not follow from the data. D) 10.2% divides the 60 ms change by the post-test mean (590) instead of the pre-test mean.
trap: Dividing by the post-test mean (590 gives 10.2%) instead of the pre-test baseline of 650 ms.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the table?

options.A: The two groups had nearly equal pre-test mean response times (650 ms and 652 ms).
options.B: The training group's accuracy rose by 7 percentage points, compared with 1 point for the control group.
options.C: The control group's post-test mean response time was lower than the training group's.
options.D: The training group's mean response time was faster at post-test than at pre-test.

explanation: Correct: C is unsupported; the control group's post-test mean RT (648 ms) was higher than the training group's (590 ms). Why the others are wrong: A) 650 versus 652 ms is nearly equal. B) 85 - 78 = 7 points and 78 - 77 = 1 point. D) The training group's mean fell from 650 to 590 ms.
trap: Reading the control group's slight 4 ms improvement as having brought it below the training group's post-test RT.

stem: The training and control groups are independent. Which analysis is most appropriate to test whether the pre-to-post change in mean response time differs between the two groups?

options.A: Chi-square test of independence on the mean RT values
options.B: Independent-samples t-test on the pre-to-post change scores (or a mixed ANOVA with group x time)
options.C: Paired t-test comparing training pre-test RT with control post-test RT
options.D: Pearson correlation between RT and accuracy

explanation: The question compares change between two independent groups, so the change scores (or the group x time interaction) are compared with an independent-samples t-test or mixed ANOVA. A chi-square test needs categorical counts, a paired test is for the same participants measured twice, and a correlation does not compare groups.
trap: Choosing a paired t-test because the data are pre/post; pairing applies within a group, but the key comparison is between independent groups.
